I now give the floor to his excellency
Odo Tei, chair of delegation of Vanuatu.
Mr. President of the General Assembly,
Mr. Secretary General,
Excellencies,
Ladies and gentlemen,
Mr. President,
I have the honor to address this
assembly on behalf of the government and
the people of the Republic of Vanuatu.
I bring with me the voice of a nation of
more than 80 islands, of many indigenous
communities and languages, and a nation
whose identity has been shaped by the
ocean, by custom, by faith, by
resilience, and above all by commitment
to peace.
Mr. Secretary General, this session also
carries a particular s significance for
us because it is the final high level
general assembly of your tenure as
secretary general of the United Nations.
On behalf of the government and people
of Anatu, I wish to convey a profound
appreciation for your service to the
United Nations and your engagement with
the people of the Pacific. Your visits
to our region reflect an understanding
that the concerns of small island
development states deserve to be heard
at a higher level. Over the course of
your tenure, you have led United Nations
through some of the most tumultuous
periods in recent international history.
You have stood consistently for
multilateralism
at a time when multilateralism itself
was under enomous pressure. Vanoatu
hopes that the next Secretary General
will carry forward that same commitment
to all member states, large or small.
Mr. President, Fenato comes to this 81st
session of the General Assembly with a
simple message. The world needs the
United Nations more than ever and the
United Nations must deliver for the
people who depend on it. The theme of
this session, restoring trust, managing
transformation, a united nations that
that delivers for all, therefore comes
at an at an important moment. The 81st
session open against a backdrop of
profound geopolitical uncertainty and
rapid transformation. For Vanoatu,
developments in international system are
never distant or abstract. The effects
reach our villages, our markets, our
schools, our hospitals, our oceans, and
our homes. Mr. President, the
international political and security
environment is becoming increasingly
difficult. We are witnessing
geopolitical competition, strategic
rivalry, armed conflicts, growing
military expenditures, economic
fragmentation, technological disruption,
and a weakening of confidence in the
multilateral institutions.
The rules that were designed to provide
predictability and stability are
increasingly being tested. The
prohibition against the use of force is
being challenged. The international
humanitarian law is being tested. The
peaceful settlements of dispute is being
undermined and the authority of
international institution is being
questioned for small states. This is
deeply concerning. Small states do not
possess the military, economic or
technological capabilities of major
powers. We do not have the ability to
impose our will through co. Our security
depends fundamentally on something else.
International law, multilateral
institutions, diplomacy, and the equal
sovereignity of states. This is why
Vanoatu has a profound interest in the
success of the United Nations. The
charter begins with a commitment to
serve succeeding generations from the
scourge of war and reaffirms the equal
rights of nations large and small. It
establishes several
It establishes sovereign equality,
peaceful settlement of disputes and the
prohibition or of the threat or or use
of force as fundamental principles of
international relations. These are not
merely legal concepts for Vanatu. They
are our security architecture.
When international law is respected, a
small nation has protection. When the
charter is respected, a small state has
a voice. When disputes are resolved
peacefully, a small state does not have
to choose between submission and
confrontation.
And when sovereignity is respected,
independence has meaning. We therefore
cannot accept a world in which
international law applies differently
according to the size, military strength
or economic power of a state. that
charter must apply equally to all. Mr.
President, the security environment is
also changing in ways that are
particularly important for the Pacific
region. The Pacific islands are
increasingly fueled through the lens of
strategic competition. There is growing
interest in our maritime spaces, our sea
lions, our resources, and our
geopolitical location. will welcome
genuine partnerships. But we also say
clearly the Pacific must not become an
arena for great power competition at the
expense of Pacific priorities. The
security of the Pacific is not simply
about military deployments or strategic
competition. For us, security also means
food security, energy security, water
security, health security, economic
security, cyber security, environmental
security, and the security of our people
from the impacts of climate change. For
Vanoatu, a cyclone that destroys a
school is a security issue. A rise in
food and energy prices as recently
experienced by Middle East conflict is a
security issue. A disrupted shipping
route is a security issue. A cyber
attack against critical infrastructure
is a security issue. Sea level rise also
resess fundamental questions on so on on
sovereignity, identity and security.
Venote joins its Pacific colleagues in
affirming the continuity of statehood
and the preservation of maritime sun and
sovereign rights in the face of sea
level rise. The rights and dignity of
affected persons must remain at the
center of international response. These
are realities faced by small island
development states. We therefore call
for a broader understanding of
international peace and security. One
that reflects the real realities of
small island developing states. And we
hope that these security concerns are
well understood here at the United
Nations. Mr. President, what happens
here in New York does not remain here in
New York. The decisions taken by major
powers affect the smallest economies. A
conflict thousands of kilometers away
can increase the price of fuel in
Vanuatu. A disruption in international
shipping can increase the price of food
in our islands. A change in global
global interest rates can increase the
cost of borrowing. A crisis in implement
in in international development finance
can delay a school, a hospital, a road
or a climate resilience project. And
global economic uncertainty can affect
tourism, investment, employment and
government revenue for Vanuatu.
Therefore, foreign policy and domestic
development are inseparable. Our
international diplomacy is is ultimately
about a people. It is about whether a
child in Tana can attend school. Whether
a farmer in Malikula can bring a produce
to market. Whether a family in Toba has
access to reliable electricity, whether
a community in Panama can recover
quickly after a natural disaster
and whether our young people can find
meaningful opportunities at home rather
rather than being forced to live in
search of them. Mr. President, this year
as Vanu celebrated its 46th independence
anniversary, we reflected on how far our
country has come since 1980. Our
independence was not given to us in a
golden plate. It was achieved through
the determination, courage, and
sacrifice of our people supported by our
brothers and sisters in the Pacific. At
our independence celebrations, we were
reminded once again of the importance of
solidarity, including the historic
support of Papa New Guinea during our
struggle for independence. Our 46th
independence anniversary was therefore
not simply a celebration of the past. It
was a call to build the future. The
message of our national celebration was
one of unity, national pride, resilience
and determination to build a stronger,
more prosperous Venatu for future
generations. And this is important in
the context of our discussions today.
Vanatu has experienced cyclones,
earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and
economic shocks and other disasters. Yet
we continue to stand. We rebuild. We
adapt and we move forward. Resilience is
not simply something Vanu speaks about.
It is something our people practice
every day. But resilience also requires
international solidarity. A small island
country cannot finance all of its
resilient needs alone. We cannot rebuild
every road, bridge, school, and hospital
after every disaster from domestic
resources alone. We cannot absorb absorb
indefinitely the economic consequences
of external shocks. And we cannot
protect our people from a changing
climate without a meaningful
international cooperation. Therefore,
when we speak about climate finance,
development finance, disaster
resilience, and sustainable development,
we are not asking merely for charity. We
are asking for partnership, fairness,
and the fulfillment of international
commitments. That part partnership must
include predictable and accessible
finance for adaptation and for
addressing loss and damage. Access to
such finance must be made easier for the
small island developing island state and
must respond to the needs of our
communities. We invite partners to
support our Pacific resilience facility
in bringing the necessary resources to
support resilience efforts in the
Pacific. At the same time, keeping 1.5°
C is vital for Pacific. In light of the
international court's advisory opinion,
we ought we urge all members to give
effect on their legal obligations
through stronger climate actions and
international cooperations.
Mr. President, we are also deeply
concerned by the developing strong El
Nino event in the Pacific which
threatens to bring more extreme heat
disrupted
rainfall, drought and flooding across
the region. For Pacific Island
countries, these are not simply
materological events. They affect food
and water security, agriculture,
fisheries, health, livelihoods, and the
resilience of already vulnerable
communities. The international community
must act before disaster strikes. We
call for stronger regional early warning
system, prepositioned humanitarian
assistance, rapid access to climate and
disaster financing, and greater
investment in resilient infrastructure
and food and water security. The Pacific
does not ask ask the world to prevent El
Nino. We ask the world to help us to
prepare for it, withstand its impacts
and recover with dignity. Mr. President,
the ocean is central to Veno's identity,
culture, food security, and prosperity.
Protection of it is essential for the
future of our people. Climate change,
damage to the ocean, and loss of
biodiversity are linked. We must address
them together. Venote welcomes the entry
into the force of the BBJ agreement. It
is an important achievement for ocean
governance and multilateral cooperation.
For a nation whose identity, culture and
prosperity are inseparable from the
ocean. The BBJ agreement represents an
important step towards protecting marine
biodiversity beyond national
jurisdiction and ensuring that the
benefits of a common ocean heritage are
shared fairly and sustainably.
Vanato stands ready to contribute to its
effective implementation and to
strengthening international cooperation
for the protection of our oceans for
generations to come. Since the agreement
entered into force on 17th January 2026
following its ratification by more than
60 states including Vanoatu and our
Pacific neighbors, the international
community community has moved into a
critical implementation phase. Watu
looks forward to the first conference of
the parties advancing the
operationalization of marine protected
areas, environmental impact assessments
and the fair and equitable sharing of
benefits from marine genetic resources.
And we call on all states yet to ratify
the agreement to do so without delay.
The implementation of the BB&J agreement
must respect sovereign rights and take
full account of the sec special
circumstances and capacity constraints
of small island developing states. It
must enable countries to participate
effectively and and equally benefit from
it. The hosting of the inaugural
Melanesian Ocean Summit in Port Mos Papa
Nigini this year arrives at the critical
juncture where one where on one hand we
are faced with daily mounting challenges
of the detrimental effects of climate
change, the alarming degradation of our
marine biodiversity, pervasive marine
pollution and the overexloitation of our
vital marine resources. Yet some of
these global issues have already
escalated to a level where ensuring
sustainability for future generations
has become a critical concern
highlighting the urgent need for
improved management of our ocean
resources. In today's world, science and
technology and economic opportunities
must also work closely with our
traditional custodians in our vast
coastal area to maintain respect for
nature. Our culture and tradition are
deeply rooted in the ocean and hence our
collective wisdom and collaboration to
address the core issues affecting our
people's livelihood livelihoods today
and rescept the future of our ocean and
communities is extremely paramount. Mr.
President, the world is entering a
period period of extraordinary
transformation. Artificial intelligence
is changing economies and societies.
Digital technologies are changing the
way governments operate. Energy systems
are changing. Global trade is changing.
Democratic demographic patterns are
changing. And climate change is
transforming the physical environment in
which many of our societies exist. The
question before us is ask is not whether
trans transformation will occur. It
will. The question is who will shape the
transformation and who will benefit from
it. For Vanoatu, the answer must be
clear. Transformation must not create a
new hierarchy between those who pro
possess technology, capital and
influence and those who merely
experience the consequences. We need an
international system in which developing
countries and small states are
participants in transformation not
simply consumers of decisions made
elsewhere. Artificial intelligence
provide one example. AI offers enormous
opportunities for education, healthcare,
public administration, agriculture,
climate forecasting, and economic
development. But without appropriate
governance, it it could also deepen
existing inequalities. Small states need
access to technology. We need digital
infrastructure. We need skills and
capacity. We need access to data and
computing. And we need a meaning
meaningful for voice in establishing the
international norms that govern that
govern emerging technologies. The
digital future must not become another
form of dependency.
Mr. President, there is a tendency to
describe small states primary in terms
of our vulnerabilities. We are small. We
are geographically dispersed. We are
economically vulnerable. We have limited
institutional capacity. We depend on
international markets. We depend on
development partners. We depend on
international shipping. We depend on
imported fuel, fueled and manufactured
goods. And yes, in many respects, we are
dependent on the international system.
But dependence must not be confused with
powerlessness. Small states can lead.
Indeed, history has shown that some of
the most important developments in
international law and global governance
have emerged because small and
vulnerable states refused to remain
silent. Fenato is proud of its
commitment to the global climate debate.
We are proud of our advocacy for climate
justice. We are proud of our role in
advancing the recognition of the legal
dimensions of climate change and we
remain commitment committed to ensuring
that the forces of those most vulnerable
to climate change ahead in international
decision making. In this vein, the FAT
government wholeheartedly thank all the
UN members who have supported us in this
journey especially here at the UN
General Assembly and International Court
of Justice. Our experience demonstrate
an important principle. Influence is not
determined solely by population,
territory or military power. Influence
can come from ideas. It can come from
moral authority. It can come from
coalition building. It can come from
persistence. It can come from
international law. And it come from the
ability to bring different regions and
groups together around a common cause.
This is the strength of the general
assembly. Every member states has a
voice. Every member state has a vote and
every member states large or small has a
responsibility to contribute. The
General Assembly is the most
representative body of the United
Nations bringing together all 193
members on the basis of sovereign
equality for countries such as Venatu.
This principle is fundamental. Mr.
President, the imposition of cohesive
economic measures, including unilateral
sanctions against developing countries,
is unfair and unjust. Such measures are
in violation with the principles
enshrined in the charter of the United
Nations and adversely affect sustainable
development outcomes of countries such
as Cuba. In this respect, we
consistently call for the uplift of the
economic embark on the Republic of Cuba.
Mr. President, peace and security cannot
be separated from human rights. Fanatu
remains deeply concerned about reports
of serious human rights violations
affecting indigenous Papuans in West
Papua. United Nations special procedures
have also raised concerns regarding
indigenous rights, displacement,
cultural rights, environmental impacts
and the treatment of human rights
defenders in Papua. The call from the
Pacific Forum leaders for the UN human
rights commissioner visit to West Papu
remains unheeded and needs to be action.
Mr. President, Vanatu reaffirms its
unwavering support for the
decolonization of Kaki New Calonia which
remains a nonselfgoverning territory
under the purview of the United Nations.
We reiterate the inelible right of the
indigenous Kanak people to
self-determination and call for a
peaceful, inclusive, transparent and
credible process consistent with the
charter of the United Nations and
relevant general assembly resolutions.
We remain concerned by the persistent
social economic disparities affecting
affecting the Canak people including
inequalities in employment, education,
income and access to economic
opportunities. These long-standing
structural imbalances continue to
constrain the full and equitable
enjoyment of economic, social, and
cultural rights by indigenous cans.
Notwithstanding the territories
considerable natural resources and
economic potential. Reports from the
Evelyn case supported by independent
assessment point to the enduring effects
of economic marginalization and uneven
development which may be understood as
forms of structural violence in so far
as they limit meaningful participation
in an inequitable benefit from the
territories development. Addressing
these disparities is essential to
fostering social cohesion and advancing
a just inclusive and sustainable
decolonization process. In this regard,
Venato calls for the full implementation
of relevant United Nation resolutions on
the question of new Calonia and
encourages continued engagement and
constructive dialogue among all
stakeholders including the
administrating power and the
representatives of the Kanak people. We
further reaffirm the important role of
the special committee on decolonization
and the fourth committee in advancing
the realization of self-determination
and sh and ensuring that the rights
aspirations and interests of the kanak
people remain at the center of
decolonization pro process. Mr.
President at the end of August the FATU
government initiated proceedings against
France before the International Court of
Justice concern concerning sovereignity
over um N and um Lea Islands or Matthew
and Hunter as they call in English and
the maritime boundaries between Vanoatu
and New Calonia. These islands are
integral part of anatu's territory
grounded in customary governance
long-standing historical connections,
indigenous ownership and is seen as part
of our duty as ancestral custodians to
protect and preserve. We recognize
France as a steadfast champion of the
international rules-based order and
under the leadership of President Mron,
a strong supporter of international
judicial institutions. France has stood
alongside Vonoatu in advancing global
climate action, including through its
support for initiative before the
International Court of Justice. We
greatly value this partnership and
France leadership on issues of
international importance. It is in the
same spirit of mutual respect and
commitment to international law that we
respectfully invite France to consent to
the jurisdiction of the court. Mr.
President, trust is important for the
United Nations credibility. It cannot be
restored through declarations alone.
Trust must be earned through action.
People will trust the United Nations
when they see it preventing conflict.
They will trust it when international
law is respected. They will trust it
when humanitarian assistance reaches
those who need it. They will trust it
when development commitments become real
projects. They will trust it when
climate finance reach vulnerable
communities. They will trust it when
small states are ahead and they will
trust it when the international system
treats all nations with equal dign
dignity. For Vanoatu, restoring trust
also means restoring confidence in the
multilateral in multilateralism itself.
We must resist the temptation to
conclude that because the international
system is imperfect, it is therefore
irrelevant. The UN80 reforms currently
implemented are paramount to rebuild
trust again at the United Nations and
therefore needs to be managed
diligently. FATU supports efforts to
strengthen the United Nations. But
reform must preserve what is most
important, the principle of sovereign
equality. The United Nations cannot
become an institution where the forces
of the most powerful states dominate,
where smaller states are expected merely
to follow. Reform must strengthen
general assembly. It must make
international institutions more
accessible to developing countries. It
must address the financing and capacity
constraints facing small delegations. It
must strengthen prevented preventive
diplomacy. It must improve
implementation of international
decisions decisions. It must ensure that
the development pillar remains resourced
and that the implementation on the
ground is effective and efficient. and
it must ensure that international law
remains central to the international
system. Forato calls for UN Security
Council that is more representative,
transparent and accountable with
membership
and working methods that reflect today's
realities and give all regions a
meaningful voice. But reform cannot be
limited to institutional structures. The
deeper reform we require is political
and renewed commitment by member states
to the principles we have already agreed
to that charter does not need to be
reinvented. It needs to be respected.
Mr. President, excellencies for veno the
United Nations charter remain our
compass. It tell it tells us that the
nations are sovereign equals. It tells
us that disputes must be settled
peacefully. It tells us that the force
must not be used against the treachery
or political independence of states. It
tells us that the nations must
cooperate. It tells us
and it reminds us that the ultimate
purpose of the international system is
not power for its own sake. It is peace,
justice, human dignity, development and
cooperation. And it is better future for
succeeding generations. These principles
are particularly important to Venuatu
because we know what independence means.
Our independence is not merely the
absence of colonial rule. Independence
means the right of our people to
determine our future. It means
sovereignity. It means dignity. It means
equality. And it means having an equal
place in the family of nations. That is
why Venat will continue to defend the
multilateral system. That is why we will
continue to defend international law and
that is why we will continue to speak
for the principle that every nation
regard regardless of size matters. Mr.
President, we meet at a critical moment
in international affairs. There are wars
that remain unresolved. There are
communities facing humanitarian
catastrophe. There's growing
geopolitical revoly. There is economic
uncertainty. There is climate
disruption. There is technological
transformation. And there is declining
confidence in the international systems
institutions. Yet I remain convinced
that this is precisely the moment when
we must choose cooperation over
confrontation. We must choose dialogue
over division. We must choose law over
force. We must choose solidarity over
indifference. And we must choose
multilateralism over fragmentation. Fatu
comes from a part of the world where our
ancestors navigated fast oceans using
the stars, the winds, the currents and
the knowledge pass from generation to
generation. Today the international
community is navigating another
uncertain ocean. We need a campus. The
United The United Nations Charter is
that compass. It provides the principles
by which we can navigate a world of
competing interest while preserving our
common humanity. The theme of this ATV
session, restoring trust, managing
transformation, a United Nations that
delivers for all reminds us of what is
required. But ultimately, restoring
trust will depend not on the watch we
adopt here, but on the actions we take
when we leave this hall. Let us
therefore build a United Nations that is
strong enough to prevent war, fair
enough to protect the vulnerable,
courageous enough to defend
international law, and inclusive enough
to give every nation a meaningful voice.
Let us build a United Nations where the
concerns of a small ally nation in the
Pacific and all over the world can stand
alongside those of the largest powers of
the world. Let us not allow division to
rule our era. Instead, we choose
cooperation. We choose peace. We choose
justice. We choose solidarity. And we
choose to renew our faith in the idea
that together nations can build a world.
We can build a better world. Vatu stands
ready to do its path. Thank you.
I thank the chair of delegation of
Vanuatu.
I would now give the floor to his
